_readme: Cross-language conformance fixture for the agent session ID rule.
WHY THIS FILE EXISTS: the worker enforces the rule (backend/util/validate/name.go,
ValidateSessionID, in sessionid.go) and the browser hand-mirrors it
(frontend/src/lib/validate.ts, validateSessionId) so the resume field can refuse a bad
token at the field instead of after a round trip. A mirror that nobody checks stops
matching. This file is that check: both suites read it, so EDITING ONE SIDE WITHOUT
THE OTHER IS THE EXACT BUG IT PREVENTS -- the language that drifts is the one whose CI
turns red. The name rule and the password rule each already have such a file; this
rule was the third hand-written class and the only one with nothing to pin it.
THE RULE REFUSES, IT DOES NOT STRIP. A session ID is an opaque token that the worker
hands to the agent: it becomes an argv element of `claude --resume <id>` and the
`sessionId` member of an ACP request. A rewritten token resumes a different session,
or no session, and the user then sees a fresh conversation with no report of why. So
the only correct answer for a character this rule does not want is to report it.
THE CLASS: valid UTF-8, no control character (the whole Cc category, U+0000-U+001F and
U+007F-U+009F), no invisible format character (the same nine ranges the name rule
strips), none of the four characters " \ $ %, no whitespace at either end, no leading
hyphen, non-empty, at most 128 UTF-8 bytes. The empty value is ACCEPTED and means 'no
resume'.
THE LEADING HYPHEN IS AN ARGV RULE, not a character rule -- a hyphen anywhere else is
ordinary and stays accepted. The worker passes the token to `claude --resume <id>` as
its own argv element. `--resume` takes an OPTIONAL value, so a parser of that shape
does not read a hyphen-prefixed token as the value: it leaves `--resume` empty and
parses the token as a flag of its own, and `--dangerously-skip-permissions` is one
argv element away. Quoting stops a SHELL from reading the token as syntax and does
nothing about the AGENT reading it as syntax. No provider issues an identifier that
starts with a hyphen, so the rule costs a real resume nothing.
THE CLASS IS FROZEN AND IT REPEATS THE NAME RULE'S LIST ON PURPOSE. The name rule
relaxed to keep " \ $ % as ordinary text, because no sink reads a stored NAME as
syntax. A token is not text a reader reads, so it keeps the narrow class. Writing the
list out twice is what stops a later change to what a NAME may hold from widening or
narrowing what a TOKEN may hold.
THE ORDER OF THE TESTS IS PART OF THE RULE, and this is why `refusal` is asserted
rather than a bare accept/refuse. The two languages disagree about which characters a
trim removes: Go's strings.TrimSpace claims U+0085 and JavaScript's
String.prototype.trim does not, while trim claims U+FEFF and TrimSpace does not. A
rule that trimmed FIRST therefore reported 'must not start or end with whitespace' on
one side and 'contains invalid characters' on the other, for one input. Both sides now
run the byte limit, then the UTF-8 test, then the character test, then the
whitespace-at-the-edge test, then the leading-hyphen test. The 'a leading byte order
mark' and 'a leading next line' cases below are what turn red if either side reorders
the first four. The two 'a leading hyphen AND ...' cases pin the last one, because a
hyphen-prefixed value can break two rules at once and must still report one message.
NOT HERE, and it cannot be: an invalid UTF-8 byte and a lone surrogate. encoding/json
rewrites an unpaired \uD800 escape to U+FFFD before Go sees it, so this file cannot
carry such an input at all -- the fixture would pin the replacement character rather
than the case. Each language pins its own half instead: TestValidateSessionIDRefusesInvalidUTF8
in Go, and the 'refuses a lone surrogate' case in the TypeScript suite. Both exist
because TextEncoder and protobuf both rewrite such a value silently, so the browser
would measure and send a token the user never typed.
CONSUMED BY (keep both in sync with this schema):
Go: backend/util/validate/sessionid_test.go  TestValidateSessionIDConformance
TS: frontend/src/lib/validate.test.ts        validateSessionId conformance block
THE CONTRACT, per case: the session ID is `text` repeated `repeat` times (`repeat` is
optional and defaults to 1; it exists so a boundary reads as the NUMBER 128 rather
than as 128 characters a reader has to count), followed by `tail` (optional). Both
sides assert:
the validator accepts the ID iff `valid`
a refused ID reports the rule named by `refusal`
`refusal` is one of `too_long`, `not_utf8`, `forbidden_character`, `whitespace_at_edge`,
`leading_hyphen`, and is empty when `valid`. Each suite maps the token to a marker in its own message,
because the two messages differ by the leading capital only.
Each case carries a `why` that says what it pins. Write a NEW case with the code
point escaped (\uXXXX) rather than the literal character, so a reader can see which
code point each case means and it stays readable in a diff.

cases.why: the empty value is accepted and means 'no resume'
an ordinary ULID token passes unchanged
a UUID with hyphens passes: the rule refuses no visible punctuation it does not name
the punctuation a base64url or an opaque provider id uses is not in the refused set
the plain U+0020 stays legal INSIDE a token; only the other whitespace goes
the plain U+0020 stays legal INSIDE a token; only the other whitespace goes
a double quote is refused. The name rule now KEEPS it, and this case is what stops that relaxation reaching the token rule
a backslash is refused, for the reason the double quote is
a dollar is refused: the token becomes an argv element, and the narrow class is cheaper than trusting every quoting layer
a percent is refused, for the reason the dollar is
a C0 control character (NUL) is refused
the top of the C0 block is refused: the range is inclusive at both ends
DEL is refused. Go's unicode.IsControl reports it, so the browser class must reach past U+007E
the C1 block is control too: Go's unicode.IsControl covers U+0080-U+009F, so the browser regex has to cover it as well
a SOFT HYPHEN is refused. It travels invisibly through a copy and a paste, and a token that carries one resumes nothing
an ARABIC LETTER MARK is refused, for the reason the soft hyphen is
a MONGOLIAN VOWEL SEPARATOR is refused. It was White_Space until Unicode 6.3 and JavaScript's \s until ES2016, so it is exactly the character a category test would answer two ways
a ZERO WIDTH SPACE is refused
a LEFT-TO-RIGHT MARK is refused: the low end of the U+200E-U+200F range
a RIGHT-TO-LEFT MARK is refused: the high end of the same range
a LEFT-TO-RIGHT EMBEDDING is refused: the low end of the U+202A-U+202E range
a RIGHT-TO-LEFT OVERRIDE is refused: the high end of the same range
a WORD JOINER is refused
a LEFT-TO-RIGHT ISOLATE is refused: the low end of the U+2066-U+2069 range
a POP DIRECTIONAL ISOLATE is refused: the high end of the same range

U+200C ZERO WIDTH NON-JOINER is ACCEPTED. The name rule keeps it because it shapes a word in Indic, Persian and Arabic orthography, and the token class matches the name rule's list exactly -- adding it here would be a one-sided widening
U+200D ZERO WIDTH JOINER is ACCEPTED, for the reason U+200C is
a variation selector is ACCEPTED: the name rule keeps U+FE00-U+FE0F, and this list follows it

a LEADING byte order mark reports the CHARACTER rule, not the whitespace rule. This case pins the ORDER: JavaScript's trim() removes U+FEFF and Go's TrimSpace keeps it, so a trim-first rule reported two different messages for this one input
a TRAILING byte order mark reports the same rule, for the same reason

a LEADING next line (U+0085) reports the CHARACTER rule. This is the mirror of the byte order mark case: Go's TrimSpace claims U+0085 and JavaScript's trim() does not, so a trim-first rule swapped the two messages here
a TRAILING next line reports the same rule, for the same reason
a leading plain space is refused, and it reaches the whitespace rule because a space is not in the character class
a trailing plain space is refused
a leading NO-BREAK SPACE is refused. This is where Go's unicode.IsSpace and JavaScript's \s have to agree, and they do
a leading IDEOGRAPHIC SPACE is refused: the one a Japanese IME emits
a value of nothing but whitespace is refused rather than treated as the empty 'no resume' value
exactly 128 bytes: the limit is inclusive, so nothing is refused
129 bytes: one byte over
43 CJK characters is 129 bytes: under a 128-CHARACTER cap and over the 128-BYTE one. A String.length count accepted this and the worker then refused it
42 CJK characters is 126 bytes, which fits. Paired with the case above, the two pin that the unit is BYTES on both sides
the byte limit is tested BEFORE the character rule, so an over-long value reports its length rather than the first bad character it happens to hold
a LEADING hyphen is refused: argv cannot tell the token from a flag, and `claude --resume` takes an optional value, so a hyphen-prefixed token parses as a flag of its own rather than as the value
the flag the rule exists to stop. One argv element is the whole attack: the token needs no space and no shell to reach the agent's own parser
a lone hyphen is refused: many parsers read it as the stdin operand
a TRAILING hyphen is accepted. Only the FIRST character is refused, so an ordinary identifier that ends in a hyphen still passes
a leading hyphen AND trailing whitespace reports the WHITESPACE rule. This case pins the ORDER: the hyphen test runs LAST on both sides, so one input gets one message
a leading hyphen AND a control character reports the CHARACTER rule: every earlier test wins, and the hyphen test is the last one
an interior LINE SEPARATOR is refused: it means what \n means, and \n is already refused as a control character
an interior PARAGRAPH SEPARATOR is refused, for the reason U+2028 is
an interior NO-BREAK SPACE is refused: it renders as a space but carries different bytes, so two tokens a reader cannot tell apart would name different sessions
an interior IDEOGRAPHIC SPACE is refused, for the reason U+00A0 is
an interior THIN SPACE is refused: the whole pinned whitespace class but the plain U+0020 goes
